newsitem.title: USA: Wells Fargo to consolidate online customers.
newsitem.headline: Wells Fargo to consolidate online customers.

text.p: Wells Fargo & Co plans to move its more than 300,000 online bank customers to Internet-based services, the bank's leading technical expert on electronic commerce said on Tuesday at the Internet Commerce Expo.

Bill Finkelstein, Wells Fargo's vice president, manager and chief scientist of Wells Fargo's direct distribution group, said the bank currently offers online channels through Prodigy Inc, as well as through the Microsoft Money and Intuit's Quicken software programs.
"We have over 300,000 online customers, of which more than half are on the Internet. The others are Quicken, Money, Prodigy and so forth," Finkelstein said.
"We are migrating our other channels all over to Internet delivery. So, within a reasonable period of time, all will be on the Internet," he added.

Wells Fargo, which claims to have the world's biggest Internet banking operation, opened its banking Website in 1995 after having garnered 20,000 online customers through an earlier service over the previous six years earlier.

"We signed up 20,000 customers between 1989 and March 1995. We signed up the second 20,000 in 14 weeks (after the new Website's launch). Today we sign up that many in two weeks or less and we're continuing to accelerate," Finkelstein said.
The Wells Fargo executive said a leading reason his bank plunged into Internet banking was the low cost of delivering high-quality service on the World Wide Web.

"It's less than one-tenth the cost of any other channel and two orders of magnitude less expensive than physical delivery," Finkelstein said. "The Internet is the least expensive way to deliver superior service that anyone has been able to figure out."

He expressed little fear of any security threat on the Internet and pointed out that Internet fraud is minimal in relationship to more traditional types of fraud that bank's face. He said the FBI's estimates that $14 billion worth of check fraud occurred in 1995.
"Our loss experience on the Internet so far after being there for two years is, like, zero," Finkelstein said.
